news_title: Vaccine Manufacturing Gap Delays NAFDAC’s WHO Level 4 Certification - LEADERSHIP Newspapers
efet_title: Vaccine Manufacturing Gap Delays NAFDAC’s WHO Level 4 Certification - LEADERSHIP Newspapers
efet_body:
The
director-general of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, said absence of local vaccine manufacturing capacity is delaying the attainment of World Health Organisation (WHO) Maturity Level 4 certification for vaccine lot release by the agency.
Adeyeye in a statement by the media consultant, Sayo Akintola, disclosed this at the 8th Nigeria Pharma Manufacturers’ Expo in Lagos, where she called on international development partners and organisations in the healthcare sector to support the establishment of vaccine manufacturing facilities in Nigeria.

She said Nigeria had made significant progress in strengthening its medicines and vaccines regulatory system and had been benchmarked in eight of the nine functions and requirements necessary to attain the relevant WHO regulatory maturity standards.
According to her, the outstanding requirement is vaccine lot release, which cannot be fully achieved without local vaccine manufacturing capacity.
The NAFDAC boss therefore urged international partners that had supported the agency’s regulatory development to extend their intervention to the establishment of fill-and-finish modular vaccine manufacturing facilities in Nigeria.
“We want to call on our international partners that have been of tremendous help. Without them we wouldn’t have been here. I want to challenge them to contribute, to fill and finish Modular Vaccine manufacturing so that we can get our Vaccine Lot Release,” she said.
Adeyeye said Nigeria already had most of the requirements needed to attain WHO Maturity Level 4 for vaccine lot release, stressing that the remaining gap was local vaccine production.
“To get Lot Release -Maturity Level 4, we have figured it out in a way we have estimated. It’s not going to cost too much. We will share that with you. Because we cannot afford to go back to where we used to be,” she said.
She recalled that Nigeria previously had the capacity to manufacture vaccines, saying the country must now rebuild that capability as part of efforts to strengthen medicine security and reduce dependence on imports.
She said, “It’s high time we went back to vaccine manufacturing.”
The NAFDAC DG also commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for the 2024 Executive Order on local pharmaceutical manufacturing, which she said had provided critical incentives to manufacturers operating under difficult economic conditions.
“I understand the stress our manufacturers are going through. Our manufacturers are patriots because they could have given up. I was championing incentives for the manufacturers until President Tinubu came on board with the Executive Order of 2024,” she said.

According to her, the executive order helped bring greater attention to the pharmaceutical and regulatory ecosystem and provided impetus for efforts to unlock value across the industry’s value chain.
She said, “nobody heard of us outside the regulatory and manufacturing industry and the gain that we have attained from regulatory and industry were not brought to the surface until the President came up with the Executive Order.”
Adeyeye added that the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare and the Minister of State for Health at the time also supported the push for incentives, which contributed to the initiative to unlock the pharmaceutical value chain.
She said the transformation of Nigeria’s pharmaceutical regulatory environment had been a gradual process, beginning with efforts to strengthen Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance among local manufacturers.
According to her, NAFDAC inspectors carried out routine GMP inspections of more than 165 companies over an eight-month period, with support from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and execution by the United States Pharmacopeia.
“We started the journey of not just the industry making products but making quality products because this is intricately tied to the way the patient’s positive health outcomes during treatment. There would not be treatment failure,” she said.
Adeyeye said the improvement in manufacturing standards had also translated into a significant reduction in the importation of products under the ‘5 plus 5’ and Ceiling Initiative between 2021 and 2025.
She said data from NAFDAC’s matrix showed that imports under the initiatives had declined by 70 per cent during the period, as local manufacturers increasingly responded to the challenge of producing quality medicines locally.

The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control has confiscated and destroyed unwholesome, banned, fake and adulterated products worth more than N8 billion in the North-Central states.
Speaking during the destruction ceremony on Thursday in Lafia, the Nasarawa State capital, the Director-General of NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, said the products were seized from manufacturing outfits, sales outlets, markets and motor parks across the zone.
The DG, who was represented by a Deputy Director of NAFDAC in the zone, Joseph Edor, said most of the confiscated products were banned alcoholic beverages in small volumes of less than 200 ml (20 cl).
According to her, NAFDAC was established by Decree No. 19 of 1993, as amended, with the mandate to protect and promote public health by ensuring that only quality, efficacious and regulated products are manufactured, imported, distributed and sold in Nigeria.
She explained that the agency banned alcoholic beverages in sachets and glass bottles of less than 200ml due to their availability, affordability and portability, which have made them easily abused by youths and underage schoolchildren.
“Research has shown that early exposure to alcohol affects the brain and other vital organs such as the liver and kidneys.
“It stymies the brain, resulting in mental retardation, brain damage, poor performance of pupils in school, low productivity and several types of illnesses,” she said.
The DG said the ban and subsequent raids were based on these abuses, addiction and adverse health effects, while other seized items included expired, fake and unwholesome food, drugs and cosmetics.
“It is in the course of carrying out these activities that this heap of unwholesome, banned, fake and adulterated products worth about eight billion naira was confiscated from manufacturing outfits, sales outlets, markets and motor parks.
“The bulk of the products in that pile are predominantly banned alcoholic beverages in low volumes of less than 200ml (20cl),” she emphasised.
The Director-General further commended other law enforcement agencies, sister agencies and stakeholders for their continuous collaboration, especially in intelligence sharing and security cover during operations.
Also speaking at the event, the Nasarawa State Coordinator of NAFDAC, Dr Gyani Stephen, explained that the exercise was not targeted at hurting people but was intended to save lives.
He advised those in the habit of selling fake and banned products to desist or be ready to face the full wrath of the law, warning that the agency would come after them if they did not change their ways.
In his goodwill message, the Nasarawa State Commander of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, Daniel Saidu, represented by Yakubu Awoh, commended NAFDAC for saving lives through the regular seizure and destruction of expired and fake drugs.
He explained that if these dangerous products were allowed into the markets, they could have destroyed millions of lives and affected the mental health of many others.

By Angela Onwuzoo
The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control has secured the conviction of a businessman, Mr Innocent Okoye, for manufacturing and selling counterfeit Goya Extra Virgin Olive Oil in Aba, Abia State, as the agency intensifies its crackdown on food adulteration and other practices that threaten public health.
Okoye, managing director of Chikason Industrial Nigeria Limited, was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, with an option of a ₦5m fine, after being found guilty on two counts relating to the production and sale of counterfeit olive oil.
According to a statement issued by NAFDAC on Thursday, Justice K. O. Ogundare of the Federal High Court, Umuahia, Abia State, delivered the judgment on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, after finding Okoye guilty on two counts relating to the manufacture and sale of counterfeit Goya Extra Virgin Olive Oil.
Okoye, identified by the agency as the Managing Director of Chikason Industrial Nigeria Limited, Aba, was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, with an option of a ₦5m fine.
The conviction followed months of investigation and prosecution arising from an enforcement operation conducted by NAFDAC’s Investigation and Enforcement Directorate in April 2026.
During the operation, the agency’s officials reportedly uncovered a facility in Aba allegedly used to produce and distribute counterfeit Goya olive oil.
The operation led to Okoye’s arrest, while samples of the products recovered from the facility were sent to NAFDAC’s laboratory for scientific analysis.
Following the investigation and laboratory examination, the agency instituted criminal proceedings against Okoye before the Federal High Court in Umuahia.
The prosecution subsequently resulted in his conviction on the two counts brought against him.
The development represents another step in NAFDAC’s efforts to hold manufacturers and distributors of counterfeit food products accountable for activities capable of exposing unsuspecting consumers to health risks.
Beyond the violation of product standards and intellectual property rights, food counterfeiting poses significant public health concerns because consumers may be unable to determine the actual ingredients, quality or safety of products fraudulently presented as genuine brands.
Counterfeit edible oils, in particular, may contain undeclared ingredients or substances produced under unhygienic conditions, exposing consumers to potentially harmful contaminants.
The risks become more pronounced when such products are consumed regularly or applied to the skin without reliable information about their composition and safety.
The conviction comes amid sustained warnings by NAFDAC over the circulation of counterfeit Goya oil in Nigerian markets. In January 2026, the agency raised the alarm over fake Goya oil packaged in polyethylene terephthalate plastic bottles and sold to unsuspecting consumers as genuine imported products.
The Director of Investigation and Enforcement at NAFDAC, Dr Martins Iluyomade, disclosed during a media briefing in Lagos that the agency had uncovered an illegal production operation at Oke-Arin Market in Idumota, Lagos. According to the agency, the operators were allegedly processing palm oil with colouring agents before repackaging the mixture as Goya oil for sale.
Iluyomade explained that the authorised Goya oil marketed in Nigeria was imported in original glass bottles through approved distribution channels, warning that products bearing the brand name in PET plastic bottles were counterfeit.
The agency consequently urged consumers, traders and religious organisations to be vigilant about the source and packaging of products offered for sale.
NAFDAC also expressed concern that counterfeiters were exploiting the popularity and widespread use of established brands to deceive consumers and profit from products whose quality and safety could not be guaranteed.

Customs seize N5.8m unregistered drugs, hand over to NAFDAC in Sokoto

By

The Nigeria Customs Service, Sokoto/Zamfara Area Command, has handed over seized unregistered pharmaceutical products worth ₦5.8m to the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control for further investigation and appropriate action.
The Acting Customs Area Controller, Deputy Comptroller Haliru Abdullahi, said the products were intercepted by Customs patrol teams along the Illela-Sokoto Road following credible intelligence.
Speaking at the handover ceremony held at the command headquarters in Sokoto on Wednesday, Abdullahi explained that the seizure formed part of efforts to stop the circulation of unregistered drugs and protect public health.
He listed the seized items as 360 packages of anti-cold drugs, 500 packages of amodiaquine, 140 packages of paracetamol and 100 packages of quinine, with a total Duty Paid Value of ₦5,804,062.06. He attributed the seizure to the commitment of the command’s patrol teams and reliable intelligence.
According to him, importing unregistered pharmaceutical products violates Section 55 of the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 and NAFDAC regulations.

He warned smugglers and dealers in such drugs to stop the illegal trade, stressing that the command would not tolerate activities that endanger public health.
“Let me use this opportunity to warn smugglers and those who deal in such unwholesome products that the Sokoto/Zamfara Command, under my watch, will not tolerate any form of smuggling.
“We remain vigilant and committed to safeguarding the health of citizens and the nation’s economy,” he said.
The acting controller praised the officers involved in the interception and acknowledged NAFDAC’s continued partnership with the Customs Service in tackling the circulation of prohibited and unregistered products.

He then handed the seized items over to NAFDAC officials.
Receiving the products on behalf of the agency, the NAFDAC State Coordinator in Sokoto, AbduSalam Lawal, commended Customs for its collaboration and efforts to rid the country of unwholesome pharmaceutical products.
He said the partnership between the two agencies was crucial to protecting Nigerians from potentially harmful medicines.
“On behalf of the Director-General of NAFDAC and the entire management of the agency, I want to express our sincere appreciation to the Nigerian Customs Service for the wonderful collaboration we’ve been enjoying,” he said.
He noted that sustained cooperation between the agencies would help keep unregistered pharmaceutical products from reaching consumers.
“This is the only way we can rid the country of some of these unwholesome products from circulation. We sincerely appreciate the efforts of your men,” Lawal said.
He also pledged NAFDAC’s commitment to strengthening the partnership with Customs to ensure that seized pharmaceutical products go through the necessary regulatory processes.
The handover highlights the role of inter-agency collaboration in combating the illegal movement of pharmaceutical products and protecting public health.
